title: Raising Kids in the Age of AI: What Every Mom Must Know
guestBio: Melinda Wittstock is a serial tech and media entrepreneur who has founded four companies to high six-, seven-, and eight-figure success. She hosts the WINGS of Inspired Business podcast, interviewing some of the most conscious women in entrepreneurship, and co-hosts the 10X Together podcast. Most recently, she stepped into the role of COO at the AI-built startup her 19-year-old son Finn founded — proof that the best leadership lessons sometimes come from your own kids.
excerpt: Tech founder Melinda Wittstock joins Aimee to talk about what AI fluency actually looks like for moms who've never written a line of code — and why the women who shape this technology will raise the kids who direct it. This is not a fear episode. It's a fluency episode.
metaDescription: Tech entrepreneur Melinda Wittstock on raising AI-fluent kids, screen boundaries, and why every mom needs to shape AI — not just react to it.
keyTakeaways: AI fluency is now a parenting skill, not just a career skill — the mothers who get curious first will raise children who build the future instead of being built by it.
You do not have to be an engineer to create with AI; you have to know what you want, and that clarity is a skill every woman already has the capacity to develop.
Critical thinking is the real protection for your kids — not restriction, not fear, and not confiscating devices, but teaching them to question what a machine confidently gets wrong.
The goal of conscious parenting in the digital age is raising creators, not passive consumers — children who direct technology rather than being directed by it.
What AI genuinely cannot replace is human connection, embodied presence, and the kind of intuitive wisdom that mothers have been practicing since the beginning of time.
Technology should be buying you more time with your people, not replacing the depth of those relationships — and that standard applies to how you allow it into your home.
Imposter syndrome does not have an age limit, and the fact that your 19-year-old feels it — or that you still feel it at 40 — is not a signal to stop; it's a signal you're growing.

pullQuotes.text: I'm not a technical person is the new I'm bad at math — and we all know how that story ended for women.
There are two futures for our kids: one where they work for AI, and one where AI works for them. Which one you raise depends on what you model right now.
The mother instinct — the ability to sense what's off before data confirms it — is exactly what's missing from the rooms where AI is being built.
Technology should buy you time with your people, not replace it. If it's doing the opposite, something has gone wrong.
It's not what you're doing that shapes your kids. It's who you're being while you do it.

content:
There is a conversation happening in the back of every mother's mind right now, and it sounds something like: Am I getting this wrong? Not in the dramatic, catastrophizing way — in the quiet, 11 p.m., staring-at-the-ceiling way. The technology is moving faster than the parenting books. The schools are not caught up. And every time you hand your kid a device to buy yourself ten minutes, there's a small, nagging voice that asks whether you're doing damage you can't yet see.

This episode is for that version of you.

Aimee sits down with Melinda Wittstock — serial tech entrepreneur, podcast host, and the COO of her own 19-year-old son's AI-built startup — for a conversation that is neither alarmist nor naive. Melinda has founded four companies, built products for audiences in the millions, and spent her career at the intersection of media and technology. But the most important credential she brings to this conversation is the same one you have: she's a mother who is figuring this out in real time, alongside her kid.

The Two Futures Sitting in Your Living Room

Melinda opens with a framework that is worth writing on a sticky note and putting somewhere you'll see it. She sees two futures for the children being raised right now: one where they work for AI, and one where AI works for them. The difference between those two futures is not IQ, not access, and not whether they went to the right school. It is fluency — the ability to direct a tool with intention rather than being passively shaped by it.

This is where Melinda lands one of the sharpest lines in the episode: "I'm not a technical person" is the new "I'm bad at math." And if you were a girl who was ever told you weren't a math person — or told yourself that story so often you stopped trying — you know exactly how much damage that kind of identity can do. AI fluency is not about writing code. It is about knowing what you want clearly enough to direct a system toward it. That is not a technical skill. That is a leadership skill. That is a you skill.

What Critical Thinking Actually Protects

One of the most practically useful parts of this conversation is Melinda's argument that restriction is not the answer — critical thinking is. AI systems are, by design, agreeable. They are built to give you a confident answer, and they will do so even when that answer is wrong. The child who grows up knowing how to question a machine, verify a claim, and sit with ambiguity long enough to find a better question is the child who will not be fooled. That skill is not taught by banning devices. It is taught by using devices together and asking out loud: wait, is that actually true?

This does not mean you hand a toddler an iPad and call it education. Melinda is clear-eyed about screen time for young children — about sleep hygiene, attention spans, and what it means to let a device parent your kid during the years when their brain architecture is still being built. The goal is not early exposure for its own sake. The goal is conscious, intentional engagement — which requires you to be present enough to model it.

The Mother Instinct Argument

Here is the part of this conversation that Aimee and Melinda both clearly believe, and that does not get said enough in technology spaces: the rooms where AI is being built are missing something, and that something is women. Not just for the optics of representation, but because the instinct that mothers specifically develop — the ability to sense what's off before any data confirms it, to hold the emotional complexity of a system, to ask what happens to the most vulnerable person in this scenario — is precisely the kind of judgment that should be shaping these tools.

If you have ever dismissed your own intuition in a professional setting because it wasn't backed by a spreadsheet, this section is going to hit differently. Your instincts are not soft data. They are often the most sophisticated pattern-recognition system in the room. And the technology that is going to touch every child alive right now desperately needs the women who have been training that system for years.

Her Son Built a Company. She Became His COO.

The story of Finn — Melinda's 19-year-old son — is one of the most compelling and quietly radical things in this episode. He had an idea in high school. He taught himself to build it using AI tools. And then he asked his mother to be his COO. Melinda said yes. What she describes is not a vanity project or a mom cheerleading from the sidelines — it is a real business, built by a teenager who learned that you don't need to know how to code; you need to know what you want to build and be willing to learn the structure around it.

The lesson she took from watching him — and the one she passes directly to you — is that the process matters as much as the product. Finn started with specs. He started with clarity about what the thing needed to do before a single line of code existed. That discipline, she argues, is the thing schools are not teaching and parents can start modeling today: think before you build, and know what problem you're actually trying to solve.

Technology Is Making Us Lonely. And It Doesn't Have To.

Melinda is also building something called Tails & Trails — a platform that uses technology to get people off their screens and into real-life community with other pet owners. It is, in her words, an example of technology being used the way it should be: not to replace human connection, but to create the conditions for it. The loneliness epidemic is real, it is measurable, and much of it was quietly accelerated by the same platforms we handed our kids without thinking too hard about the design choices baked into them.

The antidote, as she and Aimee frame it, is not to reject the technology. It is to hold the standard clearly: does this tool buy me more time with my people, or does it replace them? If the answer is the latter, something has gone wrong — and you are allowed to redesign the system, starting in your own home.

It's Who You're Being

The episode closes with a line that is simple enough to feel obvious and deep enough to stay with you. When Melinda is asked what she would tell parents raising tech-curious kids, she comes back to something that has nothing to do with devices: it's not what you're doing. It's who you're being. Your kids are not watching your screen time rules as closely as they are watching your relationship with curiosity, with failure, with the unknown. If you model a woman who gets interested instead of afraid, who asks questions instead of outsourcing answers, who stays present in the hard moments instead of disappearing into a screen — that is the education that will outlast any policy.

You do not have to have this all figured out. You do not have to become an AI expert by next Tuesday. You just have to stay in the conversation — curious, honest, and willing to learn alongside your kid. That, it turns out, is enough to change the trajectory.
